title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: saying what you mean, and why

questions.prompt: Nizar heard yesterday that his friend had failed the driving test, and this morning he put his own code book into his bag. When they meet, he says: "You'll pass it next time, and I'm going to lend you my code book." What do his two future forms express?

options.text: The first states a plan made earlier; the second predicts what will happen.
Both forms report a decision Nizar took several days ago.
The first predicts the future; the second announces a plan already made.
Both forms describe what Nizar usually does for his friends.

questions.explanation: "The first predicts the future; the second announces a plan already made." is right: You'll pass it next time is an opinion about what the future holds, one of the four jobs of will, while I'm going to lend you my code book reports an intention Nizar had formed before he opened his mouth — the book was already in his bag. "The first states a plan made earlier; the second predicts what will happen." fits each form to the wrong half of the sentence. "Both forms report a decision Nizar took several days ago." forces a plan onto You'll pass it, but nobody can plan somebody else's success. And "Both forms describe what Nizar usually does for his friends." reads them as habits, although a habit is written in the present simple, he lends his friends his books.

questions.prompt: Complete both gaps: "Hedi's e-mail was ___ concise that nobody could misunderstand it, and it was written in ___ a polite tone that his manager kept it."

options.text: such … so
so … such
so … so
such … such

questions.explanation: "so … such" is the right pair: so goes straight in front of an adjective standing on its own, as in so concise that…, while such is what you need as soon as the adjective comes with a noun, as in such a polite tone that…. "such … so" fits each word to the wrong slot. "so … so" would give so a polite tone, which is impossible, because so never accepts an article after it. And "such … such" puts such in front of the lone adjective concise, where English allows only so.

questions.prompt: Khaled announces the same news twice. To his best friend he texts: "got the job!! start sat :-) c u l8r m8". To the company he e-mails: "Dear Mrs Ben Salah, I am writing to confirm that I accept the post and that I will start on Saturday." Which feature makes the second message the formal one?

options.text: It is longer than the message he sent to his friend.
It talks about the future, while the text talks about the past.
It was written on a computer and not on a mobile phone.
It spells every word in full and keeps whole sentences.

questions.explanation: "It spells every word in full and keeps whole sentences." is the feature that decides: a formal e-mail writes see you later rather than c u l8r, I am writing rather than a bare verb, and it carries no smiley — the shortcuts and the smiley are exactly what mark the first message as private. "It is longer than the message he sent to his friend." mistakes length for register, when a formal e-mail can be very short and a text to a friend can run for pages. "It talks about the future, while the text talks about the past." is not even true, since both announce the same Saturday, and a tense never decides how formal a message is. And "It was written on a computer and not on a mobile phone." confuses the machine with the language: a perfectly formal e-mail can be written from a phone.

questions.prompt: Emna writes to the town library: "Dear Sir or Madam, I borrowed two books on 12 March and I have been ill since that day. Could I keep them one more week? I am going to bring them back on Monday 24 March." Which subject line fits her e-mail best?

options.text: Request to keep two books until 24 March
Hello from one of your regular readers :-)
Books
I am very sorry about what has happened with the two books

questions.explanation: "Request to keep two books until 24 March" is the best subject line: it is concise, and in a few words it names both what the writer wants and the date that matters, so the librarian knows what the message is about before opening it. "Hello from one of your regular readers :-)" greets instead of announcing, and a smiley has no place in a message to an institution. "Books" is concise but empty: a library receives messages about books all day long. And "I am very sorry about what has happened with the two books" reads like an apology for damage, which is not what Emna is writing about, and it is far too long for a subject line.

questions.prompt: Mouna has asked four classmates to help her carry the club's material to the bus at seven. Which answer commits its writer most firmly?

options.text: I hope to be free at seven.
I'll be at the bus at seven.
I'm going to try to come at seven.
Maybe I can be there at seven.

questions.explanation: "I'll be at the bus at seven." commits its writer most firmly: will here is a promise, and the sentence names the place and the time without a single word that leaves a way out. "I hope to be free at seven." only expresses a wish, and hoping to be free is not the same as coming. "I'm going to try to come at seven." does announce a real intention, but what the writer intends is to try, so the coming itself stays uncertain. And "Maybe I can be there at seven." adds maybe to an already weak I can, which makes it the least committing of the four.

questions.prompt: Emna is at the dentist's in Sfax and her appointment is running late. She texts her brother, who is at home two streets from the market: "The shop closes at six and I am still in the waiting room. The bread and the milk are still on the list." What is Emna asking her brother to do, without saying it directly?

options.text: To come and fetch her from the dentist's now.
To tell her what time the shop closes.
To make the list of what they need.
To buy the bread and the milk before six.

questions.explanation: "To buy the bread and the milk before six." is what Emna is really asking: she gives her brother a closing time, a reason why she cannot go herself and two items still unbought, and the only action that ties the three facts together is his going to the shop. "To come and fetch her from the dentist's now." ignores the shop and the list, which would then serve no purpose in the message. "To tell her what time the shop closes." reverses the message, since Emna is the one who gives that time. And "To make the list of what they need." comes too late: the list already exists, and the message says what is left on it.
